newsitem.title: GERMANY: Delors chides German leaders for selling EMU badly.
newsitem.headline: Delors chides German leaders for selling EMU badly.

text.p: Former European Commission president Jacques Delors chided German leaders on Tuesday for mishandling the issue of Europe's proposed single currency and worrying voters needlessly about its stability.

"They have gotten people upset with some of their arguments," Delors, who was commission president when the Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1991, told German Radio. "They have not used good arguments."
About three-quarters of Germans regularly tell opinion pollsters they oppose the plan to scrap their solid deutschemark for a euro currency they do not know.
Delors also criticised Finance Minister Theo Waigel's repeated insistence on the strictest possible interpretation of the treaty's criteria for participating countries.

The treaty says countries joining the economic and monetary union (EMU) should have budget deficits at or under three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and overall debt levels at or under 60 percent of GDP. But it also allows some leeway if a country is clearly moving in that direction.

"If one says the budget deficit cannot go over 3.00 percent -- which, by the way, goes against the spirit of the Maastricht Treaty -- then it is one's own fault if one is cornered by this," Delors said when asked about Waigel's stand.
"There is no magical number precise down to the second digit after the decimal point."

One of Germany's leading economists, Herbert Hax, called over the weekend for a delay in economic and monetary union (EMU), arguing that Bonn would in all likelihood miss the tough entry rules on budget deficits and debt that Bonn insists on.
Asked why Waigel has taken such a firm stand, Delors said the finance minister's pro-European policy faced opposition within his own Christian Social Union party in Bavaria.
"I see the polemics about the euro inside the CSU," Delors said. "If I may say so, I think what is happening there is not a good strategy."

Delors said he was sure Germany would meet the Maastricht criteria "in the spirit of the treaty" and expressed confidence that Chancellor Helmut Kohl "will convince many Germans with his usual determination".
Delors said that only countries that managed to control their public spending in the long term could join EMU: "It's not enough for a country to meet the criteria for one year."

He refused to speculate whether Italy would be part of the first wave in the EMU. "Politically, I hope Italy, Spain and Portugal will be members as soon as possible but I can't make that a condition," he said.
